claim: 108 participants with initially asymptomatic to moderate COVID-19 at diagnosis were recruited into the study.
source: We recruited 108 participants with initially asymptomatic to moderate COVID-19 at diagnosis into this study.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the manuscript describing the study cohort size and disease severity at enrollment.

source: The median age of participants was 37 years (range 18–71) with 57% male and 62% of Latinx ethnicity (Jagannathan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct demographic measurement from the study cohort with citation to the primary trial publication.

claim: 57% of participants were male.
source: The median age of participants was 37 years (range 18–71) with 57% male and 62% of Latinx ethnicity (Jagannathan et al., 2021).

claim: Eight (6.7%) participants were asymptomatic at baseline.
source: Eight (6.7%) participants were asymptomatic at baseline.

claim: The median duration of symptoms post-enrollment was 8 days.

claim: Peginterferon lambda treatment did not affect the duration of viral shedding compared with placebo.

claim: Peginterferon lambda treatment did not affect the duration of symptoms compared with placebo.

evidence: This is a direct statement of the primary trial outcome with citation to the primary trial publication.

claim: Samples at day 0 were collected a median 5 days after symptom onset (range –1 to 15).
source: Based on the subject-reported symptom starting date, samples at day 0 were collected a median 5 days after symptom onset (range –1 to 15; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct measurement of the timing of sample collection relative to symptom onset, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: There is a positive correlation between S protein-binding IgG levels at enrollment and time since symptom onset.
source: As expected, we observed a positive correlation between the S protein-binding IgG levels at enrollment and the time since symptom onset (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of an observed correlation with reference to Figure 2B showing the data.

claim: PC1 of transcriptomic data has the strongest association with time since symptom onset.
source: We found that PC1 had the strongest association with the time since symptom onset and the IgG titer, suggesting that whole blood transcriptomic profiles capture the progression of the immune response in COVID-19 patients (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the principal component analysis results with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: PC1 of transcriptomic data has the strongest association with IgG titer.
source: We found that PC1 had the strongest association with the time since symptom onset and the IgG titer, suggesting that whole blood transcriptomic profiles capture the progression of the immune response in COVID-19 patients (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the principal component analysis results with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Whole blood transcriptomic profiles capture the progression of the immune response in COVID-19 patients.
source: We found that PC1 had the strongest association with the time since symptom onset and the IgG titer, suggesting that whole blood transcriptomic profiles capture the progression of the immune response in COVID-19 patients (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the principal component analysis results, supported by the observed associations.

claim: PC2 of Olink proteomics data is highly correlated with time since symptom onset.
source: Similar to results from the analysis of transcriptomics data, Olink data were associated with disease progression, as indicated by the high correlation between PC2 and the time since symptom onset (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the principal component analysis results with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: PC1 of Olink proteomics data is associated with age.
source: We also observed an association between PC1 and age, which captures the impact of age on the plasma protein landscape in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the principal component analysis results.

claim: Transcriptional and proteomics profiles at day 5 post-treatment were similar between Peginterferon lambda and placebo treatment arms.
source: PCA revealed that transcriptional and proteomics profiles at day 5 post-treatment were similar between Peginterferon lambda and placebo treatment arms (Figure 2D and G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the PCA results comparing treatment arms with reference to figures.

claim: There were no significant differences in blood transcription modules between Peginterferon lambda and placebo groups.
source: There were no significant differences in blood transcription modules (BTMs) between groups, and only two plasma proteins (HSD1B1 and LAMP3) were significantly affected by Peginterferon lambda treatment (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results comparing treatment groups with reference to a figure.

claim: Only two plasma proteins (HSD1B1 and LAMP3) were significantly affected by Peginterferon lambda treatment.
source: There were no significant differences in blood transcription modules (BTMs) between groups, and only two plasma proteins (HSD1B1 and LAMP3) were significantly affected by Peginterferon lambda treatment (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: There were no significant differences in SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses at day 28 between Peginterferon lambda and placebo treatment arms.
source: Furthermore, we found no significant differences in SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses (at day 28 after enrollment) and antibody responses (at day 28 and month 7 after enrollment) between the two treatment arms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as reported previously (Chakraborty et al., 2021; van der Ploeg et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results with reference to a figure and citations to previous publications.

claim: There were no significant differences in antibody responses at day 28 and month 7 between Peginterferon lambda and placebo treatment arms.
source: Furthermore, we found no significant differences in SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses (at day 28 after enrollment) and antibody responses (at day 28 and month 7 after enrollment) between the two treatment arms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as reported previously (Chakraborty et al., 2021; van der Ploeg et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results with reference to a figure and citations to previous publications.

claim: Peginterferon lambda treatment did not show substantial effects on the immune response in COVID-19 outpatients.
source: Taken together, Peginterferon lambda treatment did not show substantial effects on the immune response in COVID-19 outpatients.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the multiple analyses showing no significant differences between treatment arms.

claim: 15 immune modules and 10 plasma proteins varied significantly as a function of time since symptom onset (FDR <0.05).
source: We identified 15 immune modules and 10 plasma proteins that varied as a function of time since symptom onset (false discovery rate [FDR] <0.05; Figure 3A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results with reference to a figure and supplementary file.

claim: 16 immune modules or proteins showed non-linear dynamics as indicated by significant coefficients of the quadratic term.
source: Among them, 16 immune modules or proteins showed non-linear dynamics, as indicated by significant coefficients of the quadratic term (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Four clusters of immune modules and proteins were identified based on their trajectory patterns.
source: We performed clustering analysis and identified four clusters based on the trajectory of the significant modules and proteins (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the clustering analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: Cluster 1 contains IFN-related modules and proteins known to be activated by IFN signaling, including MCP-1, MCP-2, CXCL10, and CXCL11.
source: Cluster 1 contains IFN-related modules and proteins known to be activated by IFN signaling, including MCP-1, MCP-2, CXCL10, and CXCL11 (Lehmann et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2009; Moll et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the composition of cluster 1 with citations to literature supporting the IFN-activation of these proteins.

claim: Cluster 1 trajectories peaked at the time of symptom onset and monotonically decreased over time.
source: The trajectories in cluster 1 already reached the peak at the time of symptom onset and monotonically decreased over time.
evidence: This is a direct description of the temporal pattern observed in cluster 1 trajectories.

claim: Cluster 2 trajectories peaked at 1–5 days after symptom onset.
source: The trajectories in cluster 2 peaked at 1–5 days after symptom onset and contain IFN-γ and modules related to T cell activation.
evidence: This is a direct description of the temporal pattern observed in cluster 2 trajectories.

claim: Cluster 2 contains IFN-γ and modules related to T cell activation.
source: The trajectories in cluster 2 peaked at 1–5 days after symptom onset and contain IFN-γ and modules related to T cell activation.
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the composition of cluster 2.

claim: Cluster 2 contains several myeloid cell attracting chemokines (CXCL1 and CXCL6) and innate cell response modules.
source: Interestingly, it also contains several myeloid cell attracting chemokines (CXCL1 and CXCL6) and the innate cell response modules.
evidence: This is a direct statement describing additional components of cluster 2.

claim: Cluster 3 peaked between 10 and 14 days after symptom onset and is characterized by modules related to B cells.
source: Cluster 3 peaked between 10 and 14 days after the symptom onset and is characterized by modules related to B cells.
evidence: This is a direct description of the temporal pattern and composition of cluster 3.

claim: Cluster 4 trajectories monotonically increase after symptom onset and are characterized by increasing S protein-binding IgG level and related plasma B cell modules.
source: Cluster 4 trajectories monotonically increase after symptom onset and are characterized by the increasing S protein-binding IgG level and related plasma B cell modules.
evidence: This is a direct description of the temporal pattern and composition of cluster 4.

claim: The trajectory analysis revealed sequential activation of IFN signaling, myeloid cells, IFN-γ, T cells, B cell, and antibody production within the first 15 days of symptom onset.
source: The trajectory analysis revealed the sequential activation of IFN signaling, myeloid cells, IFN-γ, T cells, B cell, and antibody production within the first 15 days of symptom onset.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the trajectory analysis results describing the temporal sequence of immune activation.

claim: The immune trajectories of the two individual treatment arms were similar to the trajectories of the combined dataset.
source: The immune trajectories of the two individual treatment arms were similar to the trajectories of the combined dataset (Figure 3A), suggesting that Peginterferon lambda treatment does not significantly affect early immune trajectories after COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing trajectories between treatment arms with reference to a figure.

claim: Peginterferon lambda treatment does not significantly affect early immune trajectories after COVID-19 infection.
source: The immune trajectories of the two individual treatment arms were similar to the trajectories of the combined dataset (Figure 3A), suggesting that Peginterferon lambda treatment does not significantly affect early immune trajectories after COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of trajectories between treatment arms.

claim: Quadratic regression did not find significant associations between major cell types and time since symptom onset.
source: Quadratic regression did not find significant associations between the major cell types and the time since symptom onset (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: The trajectories of different immune modules are mainly driven by the activation of corresponding immune cells rather than the composition change of major immune cell types.
source: The results suggest that the trajectories of different immune modules (Figure 3A) are mainly driven by the activation of corresponding immune cells rather than the composition change of major immune cell types.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results showing no change in cell composition but changes in immune modules.

claim: Eight patients with initially mild to moderate symptoms later developed progressive and more severe symptoms and presented to the emergency department or were hospitalized.
source: However, eight patients with initially mild to moderate symptoms later developed progressive and more severe symptoms and presented to the emergency department or were hospitalized (median 2 days to progression, range 1–13 days; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the number of patients who experienced disease progression with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The median time to disease progression was 2 days (range 1–13 days).
source: However, eight patients with initially mild to moderate symptoms later developed progressive and more severe symptoms and presented to the emergency department or were hospitalized (median 2 days to progression, range 1–13 days; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement of the time to disease progression with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Lymphocyte percentages were negatively correlated with symptom severity.
source: As two positive controls, we confirmed well-documented findings that lymphocyte percentages were negatively correlated with symptom severity, and neutrophil percentages were positively correlated with symptom severity (Figure 4A; Goyal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results with reference to a figure and citation to literature.

claim: Neutrophil percentages were positively correlated with symptom severity.
source: As two positive controls, we confirmed well-documented findings that lymphocyte percentages were negatively correlated with symptom severity, and neutrophil percentages were positively correlated with symptom severity (Figure 4A; Goyal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results with reference to a figure and citation to literature.

claim: Four immune modules and 25 plasma proteins were significantly associated with disease progression (FDR <0.05).
source: In addition, our regression analysis identified four immune modules and 25 plasma proteins that were significantly associated with disease progression (FDR <0.05, Figure 4B–C, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary data.

claim: Proteins and modules from cluster 1, including type I IFN response, RIG-I signaling, and multiple proteins induced by IFN signaling (CXCL10, MCP-1, MCP-2, and CXCL11), were significantly enriched in individuals who experienced disease progression.
source: The proteins and modules from cluster 1 (as identified above in Figure 3A), including the type I IFN response, RIG-I signaling, and multiple proteins known to be induced by IFN signaling including CXCL10 (also known as IFN gamma-induced protein, IP-10), MCP-1, MCP-2, and CXCL11, were significantly enriched in individuals who experienced disease progression vs. non-progressors (Fisher's exact test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the enrichment analysis results with reference to a figure and statistical test.

claim: Early innate immune activation is associated with disease progression.
source: Together, these data highlight an association between early innate immune activation and disease progression.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the results showing associations between innate immune markers and disease progression.

claim: 38 plasma proteins were significantly associated with oropharyngeal viral load.
source: We identified 38 plasma proteins significantly associated with oropharyngeal viral load (top 10 significant proteins shown in Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to a figure and supplementary data.

claim: Higher levels of RIG-I (gene symbol DDX58) were inversely correlated with viral load.
source: Higher levels of several of these proteins were inversely correlated with viral load, including the cytosolic RNA sensor RIG-I (gene symbol DDX58), chemokines (CCL20 and CCL25), and other proteins (Keratin 19 [KRT19], amphiregulin [AREG]) previously shown to be upregulated in COVID-19 patients (Talla et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results with citation to literature.

claim: Higher levels of chemokines CCL20 and CCL25 were inversely correlated with viral load.
source: Higher levels of several of these proteins were inversely correlated with viral load, including the cytosolic RNA sensor RIG-I (gene symbol DDX58), chemokines (CCL20 and CCL25), and other proteins (Keratin 19 [KRT19], amphiregulin [AREG]) previously shown to be upregulated in COVID-19 patients (Talla et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results with citation to literature.

claim: Higher levels of KRT19 and AREG were inversely correlated with viral load.
source: Higher levels of several of these proteins were inversely correlated with viral load, including the cytosolic RNA sensor RIG-I (gene symbol DDX58), chemokines (CCL20 and CCL25), and other proteins (Keratin 19 [KRT19], amphiregulin [AREG]) previously shown to be upregulated in COVID-19 patients (Talla et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results with citation to literature.

claim: Higher levels of CLEC4C and TRAIL were associated with higher oropharyngeal viral loads.
source: In contrast, higher levels of C-type lectin domain family 4 member C (CLEC4C, expressed by plasmacytoid dendritic cells) and TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) were associated with higher oropharyngeal viral loads.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results.

claim: 86 plasma proteins were significantly associated with SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses at day 28.
source: We identified 86 plasma proteins that were significantly associated with SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses at day 28, and 83 and 55 plasma proteins significantly associated with S protein-binding IgG at day 28 and month 7, respectively (top 10 significant proteins shown in Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to a figure and supplementary data.

claim: 83 plasma proteins were significantly associated with S protein-binding IgG at day 28.
source: We identified 86 plasma proteins that were significantly associated with SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses at day 28, and 83 and 55 plasma proteins significantly associated with S protein-binding IgG at day 28 and month 7, respectively (top 10 significant proteins shown in Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to a figure and supplementary data.

claim: 55 plasma proteins were significantly associated with S protein-binding IgG at month 7.
source: We identified 86 plasma proteins that were significantly associated with SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses at day 28, and 83 and 55 plasma proteins significantly associated with S protein-binding IgG at day 28 and month 7, respectively (top 10 significant proteins shown in Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to a figure and supplementary data.

claim: Several proteins including RIG-I, CXCL11, KRT19, and AREG were associated with higher levels of SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells and antibody response.
source: Several proteins were associated with higher levels of SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells and the antibody response, including RIG-I (gene symbol DDX58), chemokines (CXCL11), and other proteins (KRT19 and AREG) also associated with control of viral load (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: 20 plasma proteins were correlated with three out of four patient outcomes.
source: Altogether, we identified 20 plasma proteins that were correlated with three out of four patient outcomes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the overlap analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Higher plasma levels of RIG-I were significantly associated with all examined clinical, virological, and immunological outcomes.
source: Interestingly, higher plasma levels of RIG-I (gene symbol DDX58) were significantly associated with all examined clinical, virological, and immunological outcomes (Figure 5C), including disease progression, lower oropharyngeal viral load, increased SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses, and increased levels of S protein-binding IgG to SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: Plasma RIG-I levels were only modestly correlated with mRNA-level expression of RIG-I (correlation = 0.23, p value=0.004).
source: We found that the plasma RIG-I levels were only modestly correlated with mRNA-level expression of RIG-I (correlation = 0.23, p value=0.004, Figure 5D), as well as RIG-I signaling and IFN-related modules (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: There is a strong correlation between plasma levels of RIG-I and plasma levels of DFFA.
source: In contrast, we found a strong correlation between plasma levels of RIG-I and plasma levels of DNA Fragmentation Factor Subunit Alpha (DFFA), an intracellular protein known to be involved in apoptosis (Figure 5H; Thomas et al., 2000; Zhang and Xu, 2000).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results with reference to a figure and citations to literature.

claim: DFFA is an intracellular protein known to be involved in apoptosis.
source: In contrast, we found a strong correlation between plasma levels of RIG-I and plasma levels of DNA Fragmentation Factor Subunit Alpha (DFFA), an intracellular protein known to be involved in apoptosis (Figure 5H; Thomas et al., 2000; Zhang and Xu, 2000).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge with citations to literature.

claim: Many plasma proteins correlated with plasma RIG-I levels were intracellular proteins.
source: In addition, many of the other plasma proteins correlated with plasma RIG-I levels were intracellular proteins (Figure 5E), suggesting that plasma RIG-I levels may be driven by both increased intracellular RIG-I expression, as well as a cell death process that releases intracellular protein into the plasma.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: Plasma RIG-I levels may be driven by both increased intracellular RIG-I expression and a cell death process that releases intracellular protein into the plasma.
source: In addition, many of the other plasma proteins correlated with plasma RIG-I levels were intracellular proteins (Figure 5E), suggesting that plasma RIG-I levels may be driven by both increased intracellular RIG-I expression, as well as a cell death process that releases intracellular protein into the plasma.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlation between plasma RIG-I and intracellular proteins.

claim: Plasma levels of RIG-I were not significantly associated with time since symptom onset.
source: As plasma levels of RIG-I were not significantly associated with time since symptom onset (Supplementary file 2), these data suggest that plasma RIG-I levels might serve as a powerful and stable biomarker for predicting several clinical, virological, and immunological outcomes in patients with COVID-19.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the regression analysis results with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Plasma RIG-I levels might serve as a powerful and stable biomarker for predicting several clinical, virological, and immunological outcomes in patients with COVID-19.
source: As plasma levels of RIG-I were not significantly associated with time since symptom onset (Supplementary file 2), these data suggest that plasma RIG-I levels might serve as a powerful and stable biomarker for predicting several clinical, virological, and immunological outcomes in patients with COVID-19.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the stability of RIG-I levels over time and their associations with multiple outcomes.

claim: The immune response after the first dose of BNT162b2 vaccination largely mirrors the trajectory of immune response after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Comparison of the datasets reveals that the immune response after the first dose of vaccination (day 0 to day 21) largely mirrors the trajectory of immune response after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing the immune trajectories between vaccination and infection.

claim: Early proteins and BTMs in SARS-CoV-2 infection, including IFNγ, MCP1, CXCL11, MCP2, CXCL10, and IFN-related transcriptional modules, are upregulated within the first 7 days of vaccination.
source: Early proteins and BTMs in the SARS-CoV-2 infection dataset, including IFNγ, MCP1, CXCL11, MCP2, CXCL10, and IFN-related transcriptional modules, are upregulated within the first 7 days of the vaccination.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing the timing of immune marker upregulation between infection and vaccination.

claim: Late immune markers in SARS-CoV-2 infection, including SLAMF1, TNFRSF9, CCL3, CCL4, TGFα, TNFSF14, and B cell-related transcriptional modules, are upregulated 21 days after vaccination.
source: Late immune markers in the SARS-CoV-2 infection dataset, including SLAMF1, TNFRSF9, CCL3, CCL4, TGFα, TNFSF14, and B cell-related transcriptional modules, are upregulated much later and show highest levels 21 days after the vaccination (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing the timing of immune marker upregulation between infection and vaccination with reference to figures.

claim: The response after the second dose of vaccine is characterized by fast upregulation of both early and late immune measurements.
source: In contrast, the response after the second dose of vaccine (day 22 to day 28) is characterized by fast upregulation of both early and late immune measurements (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the immune response after the second vaccine dose with reference to figures.

claim: Three proteins (TRAIL, CXCL1, and CXCL6) that are significantly upregulated in SARS-CoV-2 patients were not induced after the second dose of vaccine.
source: Interestingly, three proteins that are significantly upregulated in SARS-CoV-2 patients were not induced after the second dose of vaccine, including TRAIL, CXCL1, and CXCL6.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing protein expression between infection and vaccination.

claim: TRAIL, CXCL1, and CXCL6 are highly expressed in neutrophils.
source: All three proteins are highly expressed in neutrophils (Uhlén et al., 2015) and have been shown to regulate neutrophil recruitment (CXCL1 and CXCL6) or apoptosis (TRAIL) during inflammation (Jovic et al., 2016; Sawant et al., 2016; Renshaw et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge with citations to literature.

claim: CXCL1 and CXCL6 regulate neutrophil recruitment during inflammation.
source: All three proteins are highly expressed in neutrophils (Uhlén et al., 2015) and have been shown to regulate neutrophil recruitment (CXCL1 and CXCL6) or apoptosis (TRAIL) during inflammation (Jovic et al., 2016; Sawant et al., 2016; Renshaw et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge with citations to literature.

claim: TRAIL regulates neutrophil apoptosis during inflammation.
source: All three proteins are highly expressed in neutrophils (Uhlén et al., 2015) and have been shown to regulate neutrophil recruitment (CXCL1 and CXCL6) or apoptosis (TRAIL) during inflammation (Jovic et al., 2016; Sawant et al., 2016; Renshaw et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge with citations to literature.

claim: The lack of TRAIL, CXCL1, and CXCL6 suggests an absence of neutrophil response to the second dose of vaccine.
source: The lack of TRAIL, CXCL1, and CXCL6 suggests an absence of neutrophil response to the second dose of vaccine.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the absence of neutrophil-associated proteins after the second vaccine dose.

claim: Associations identified in the vaccine dataset are largely consistent with associations identified in the COVID-19 infection dataset.
source: We next examined associations between plasma proteins and immunological outcomes of BNT162b2 vaccination. The associations identified in the vaccine dataset are largely consistent with the associations identified in the COVID-19 infection dataset (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing associations between the two datasets with reference to a figure.

claim: Proteins associated with T cell responses after infection (CXCL9 and CXCL10) were also associated with T cell responses after vaccination.
source: In particular, proteins that are associated with the T cell (CXCL9 and CXCL10) and antibody responses (INF-γ, MCP1, L10, PDL1, CXCL10, ADA, and CXCL11) after infection were also associated with the T cell and antibody responses after vaccination, highlighting important similarities between infection- and vaccine-induced immunity.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing associations between infection and vaccination.

claim: Proteins associated with antibody responses after infection (INF-γ, MCP1, L10, PDL1, CXCL10, ADA, and CXCL11) were also associated with antibody responses after vaccination.
source: In particular, proteins that are associated with the T cell (CXCL9 and CXCL10) and antibody responses (INF-γ, MCP1, L10, PDL1, CXCL10, ADA, and CXCL11) after infection were also associated with the T cell and antibody responses after vaccination, highlighting important similarities between infection- and vaccine-induced immunity.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing associations between infection and vaccination.

claim: Plasma biomarkers may be useful correlates of protective immunity following both natural infection and vaccination.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that these plasma biomarkers may be useful correlates of protective immunity following both natural infection and vaccination.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the shared associations between infection and vaccination.

claim: Machine learning models using 2-7 protein markers achieved cross-validation AUC of 0.87 for predicting disease progression.
source: The final models achieved cross-validation AUC of 0.87, 0.78, 0.72, 0.81, and 0.77 for predicting disease progression, oropharyngeal viral load, day 28 SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cell responses, day 28 S protein-binding IgG levels and month 7 S protein-binding IgG levels, respectively (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the machine learning model performance with reference to a figure.

evidence: This is a direct statement of the machine learning model performance with reference to a figure.

evidence: This is a direct statement of the machine learning model performance with reference to a figure.

source: The final models achieved cross-validation AUC of 0.87, 0.78, 0.72, 0.81, and 0.77 for predicting disease progression, oropharyngeal viral load, day 28 SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cell responses, day 28 S protein-binding IgG levels and month 7 S protein-binding IgG levels, respectively (Figure 7B).

claim: Machine learning models using 2-7 protein markers achieved cross-validation AUC of 0.77 for predicting month 7 S protein-binding IgG levels.
source: The final models achieved cross-validation AUC of 0.87, 0.78, 0.72, 0.81, and 0.77 for predicting disease progression, oropharyngeal viral load, day 28 SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cell responses, day 28 S protein-binding IgG levels and month 7 S protein-binding IgG levels, respectively (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the machine learning model performance with reference to a figure.

claim: Selected protein markers substantially improved the prediction of disease progression compared to demographic and comorbidity data alone.
source: We compared the final models to baseline models that use only demographic (age and gender) and comorbidity (hypertension, diabetes, and obesity) data. The selected protein markers substantially improved the prediction of disease progression, S protein-binding IgG levels at day 28 and month 7, and oropharyngeal viral load.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing model performance with and without protein markers.

claim: Selected protein markers substantially improved the prediction of S protein-binding IgG levels at day 28 and month 7 compared to demographic and comorbidity data alone.
source: We compared the final models to baseline models that use only demographic (age and gender) and comorbidity (hypertension, diabetes, and obesity) data. The selected protein markers substantially improved the prediction of disease progression, S protein-binding IgG levels at day 28 and month 7, and oropharyngeal viral load.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing model performance with and without protein markers.

evidence: This is a direct statement of the validation results in an independent dataset with reference to a figure.

claim: The machine learning model was able to accurately identify severe cases in an independent dataset from Patel et al., achieving an AUC of 0.85.
